what_it_is.body: Celo is an Ethereum Layer 2 focused on payments and real-world applications. It began as a standalone proof-of-stake Layer 1, then migrated the same history and state to an OP Stack Optimium on March 26, 2025. CELO is still the gas and governance asset. Current Celo therefore has continuity with the old chain, but a different security and operating model.

what_happened.body: Celo reached $1.15 billion of TVL in October 2021, when it was still an L1. TVL was $14.35 million at review, 98.76% below that peak. Dollar stablecoins were $107.26 million and thirty-day DEX volume was $94.22 million, down 65.36% from the prior provider comparison. Fees were $62,382.69 and retained revenue was $25,299.47.

why_this_outcome.body: Celo chose to preserve its mobile-payment brand, CELO economy and application history while replacing a small independent validator economy with Ethereum settlement and cheaper rollup operations. The move supported high transaction activity and a stablecoin base that is much larger than DeFi TVL. It did not restore the capital and token valuations reached during the 2021 cycle. The result is an active payments-oriented L2 with declining capital-market outcomes.

strategic_choices.body: Celo made three consequential choices: migrate the existing L1 state into an Ethereum L2; use EigenDA with Ethereum fallback instead of posting all transaction data directly to Ethereum; and retain CELO rewards and community RPC providers after validators stopped securing consensus. It later added OP Succinct Lite proofs, while keeping whitelisted proposers and challengers and instant upgrade paths.

operating_model.body: A centralized sequencer orders Celo transactions. State roots are proposed to Ethereum, and OP Succinct Lite lets valid ZK proofs resolve challenged states, but proposers and at least five challengers are permissioned. Transaction data is posted to EigenDA, with an Ethereum fallback. Community RPC providers receive CELO rewards, but they are not the consensus validators that secured the former L1.

token_and_value_capture.body: CELO pays gas, supports governance, backs network rewards and retains token duality on the L2. The bridge represents a fixed one-billion CELO supply across Ethereum and Celo rather than creating two independent supplies. CoinGecko observed CELO at $0.061327 with a $37.10 million market capitalization and $61.29 million fully diluted value, 99.38% below its recorded high.

counterfactual.body: Celo could have remained an independent L1, preserving validator consensus but carrying the cost of securing and maintaining a smaller base layer. It could have launched a fresh L2 and left the old state behind, simplifying the boundary but fragmenting users and history. It could also post all data to Ethereum and remove permissioned roles, improving trust assumptions at a higher operating cost.

risks_and_unknowns.body: Users face sequencer, proposer, challenger, external-data and instant-upgrade dependencies. L2BEAT reports no exit window for unwanted upgrades and says withdrawals can freeze if permissioned proposers stop. Historical TVL also crosses an L1-to-L2 boundary, so the drawdown is economically useful but not a like-for-like security comparison. We still lack durable payment-user cohorts and a complete entity-level control map.

lifecycle.body: Celo is operating but declining. The L2 migration and proof upgrade shipped, activity is high and stablecoin supply is meaningful. At the same time, TVL is 98.76% below its L1-era peak, DEX volume fell 65.36% month over month and CELO is 99.38% below its high. The chain survived by changing architecture; the open question is whether payment demand can create durable fees and token value.

outlook_and_watch.body: The base case is a high-activity, low-cost payments L2 whose stablecoin use remains larger than its DeFi capital base. The call improves if repeat payment users, fees and TVL grow without heavier subsidies, and if proposers, challengers and upgrades become less permissioned. Watch stablecoin transfers, retained wallets, DEX volume, bridge flows, CELO issuance, proof disputes, EigenDA fallback and governance-control changes.

outcome.summary: Celo successfully migrated a live community to an active Ethereum L2, but capital, monthly trading and CELO remain far below their peaks. Payment activity survives; the capital-market outcome is declining.

why.summary: Preserving the ledger, token and payment distribution reduced migration disruption, while external data and permissioned operation lowered cost. Those choices kept use alive without restoring 2021 capital and token demand.

what_it_is.body: Doma is a chain and protocol for turning traditional internet domains into programmable onchain assets. Registrars remain responsible for registrations, DNS and ICANN compliance; Doma records and moves tokenized representations. The Doma app is a portfolio and marketplace interface, while Interstellar is a registrar. Doma Chain uses ETH for gas and has no verified native DOMA token.

what_happened.body: Doma mainnet launched on November 25, 2025 with two flagship tokenized domains and registrar partnerships covering more than 30 million domains that were capable of being tokenized. That is potential inventory, not 30 million onchain domains. TVL was $821,886, only 0.02% below its short-history peak. Thirty-day DEX volume was $73.66 million, up 16.37%, while fees were $28,746 and provider-reported revenue was zero.

why_this_outcome.body: Doma found a distinct distribution route through registrars that already control domain customer relationships. Tokenization and fractional liquidity can make expensive domains easier to trade, which helps explain volume far above the small TVL base. But the network is new, revenue is unproven and domain ownership still depends on offchain registrar records. The result is middling: real product and activity, without enough history to call durable success.

strategic_choices.body: Doma chose to work through registrars instead of trying to replace DNS authority. It built a dedicated chain and common integration layer, then made assets portable to supported chains. It uses ETH for gas rather than requiring a new network token. Interstellar acts as a reference registrar, while the Doma app aggregates assets across registrars. Future-TLD Name Tokens remain reservations, not approved DNS domains.

operating_model.body: A registrar tokenizes a domain and keeps the authoritative customer and DNS records. Doma Chain and connected smart contracts track the onchain asset, offers, transfers and cross-chain state. Users sign onchain actions, but the registrar must synchronize official ownership and can remain decisive when a domain expires, is disputed or changes offchain. Current materials name Conduit, Celestia and messaging partners, but do not provide a complete public sequencer, upgrade or bridge-control map.

token_and_value_capture.body: Doma Chain charges gas in ETH. Domain owners can create domain-backed tokens and liquidity pools, but those are assets tied to particular domains, not a network token. Doma Points have no cash value, property rights or guaranteed future token utility under the current terms. Value capture therefore depends on domain-market fees, services and ecosystem activity; provider data did not show retained protocol revenue for the reviewed month.

counterfactual.body: Doma could have built only a multichain contract standard and avoided its own chain, reducing infrastructure while losing a shared registry and marketplace hub. It could have issued a native token, creating validator or incentive tools but adding speculation and dilution. It could also bypass registrars, increasing onchain autonomy while losing authoritative DNS synchronization and regulatory distribution.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The hard problem is keeping registrar, DNS, wallet and token state consistent. Expiration, trademark disputes, transfers, account recovery, bridge failures and smart-contract bugs can break the link between an onchain token and usable domain rights. High volume may come from a few fractional pools rather than many domain buyers. We lack unique-buyer retention, actual tokenized-domain counts, liquidity depth, operator control and a reconciliation from fees to retained revenue.

lifecycle.body: Doma is operating and middling. It has a live mainnet, working registrar integrations, near-peak TVL and rising monthly trading. It also has less than one year of market history, under $1 million of TVL and no provider-reported retained revenue. This is a credible product experiment with early activity, not yet proof that domains become deep, repeat financial markets.

outlook_and_watch.body: The base case is a niche DomainFi network that succeeds when registrars supply high-quality inventory and buyers return after initial launches. The call improves if the number of usable tokenized domains, unique repeat buyers, liquidity depth and retained fees grow together without ownership disputes. Watch domain expirations, registrar additions, bridge incidents, wallet recovery, pool concentration, net revenue and the gap between partner inventory and assets actually onchain.

what_it_is.body: Fraxtal is currently an EVM-equivalent OP Stack Layer 2 on Ethereum. It uses custom FraxtalDA, FRAX for gas and Flox incentives for users and contracts. Some Frax documentation describes a future or upgraded “Fraxtal L1,” but the current network page and independent risk analysis still identify the live chain as an L2. FXTL is currently a points ledger, not a verified freely traded network token.

what_happened.body: Fraxtal reached $87.98 million of TVL on February 1, 2025. TVL was $18.32 million at review, a 79.18% drawdown. Dollar stablecoins were $10.12 million. Thirty-day DEX volume rebounded 461.43% to $4.01 million from a low comparison base, while fees were $8,780.36 and retained revenue was $796.29. L2BEAT reported only about 0.24 user operations per second.

why_this_outcome.body: Fraxtal had a built-in distribution advantage: Frax assets, applications and users could move onto a chain designed around the same ecosystem. Flox paid both gas spenders and the contracts they used, creating reasons to transact. That did not retain most peak capital, and current usage and revenue remain modest. Custom data availability, no functional proof system and frequent token-language changes add trust and comprehension costs. The shipped chain is active but declining.

strategic_choices.body: Fraxtal chose OP Stack execution with its own offchain data layer. It replaced frxETH gas with FRAX through the FXS-to-FRAX upgrade, added an inflationary tail-emission schedule, and rewards both users and contracts through Flox and FXTL accounting. Those choices tightly integrate the Frax economy and subsidize activity. They also concentrate infrastructure, expand supply and make token identities harder for users to follow.

operating_model.body: A permissioned sequencer orders Fraxtal transactions and posts data commitments to Ethereum. FraxtalDA stores data across AWS, IPFS and Cloudflare R2, but L2BEAT identifies one DA endpoint and no DA bridge that proves inclusion on Ethereum. The proof system is not functional, so invalid state roots can be accepted. Only whitelisted proposers publish roots; users can force transactions through Ethereum after a delay, but proposer failure can freeze withdrawals.

token_and_value_capture.body: FRAX is the live gas asset. Since April 28, 2025, holders can bridge legacy FXS 1:1 into FRAX; WFRAX is its ERC-20 wrapper. FRAX supply follows an 8% annual tail emission that is scheduled to fall to a 3% floor, while base-fee burns offset part of issuance. FXTL remains points. The old promise to tokenize FXTL within twelve months of genesis is past due in the current documentation, so it cannot be presented as a completed token launch.

counterfactual.body: Fraxtal could post all data to Ethereum and deploy permissionless proofs, increasing cost while reducing operator trust. It could have kept frxETH as gas or retained the FXS name, avoiding another asset migration but weakening the single-token strategy. It could reward usage only from realized fees instead of tail emissions, reducing subsidies while making early growth harder.

risks_and_unknowns.body: Fraxtal depends on a permissioned sequencer and proposer, custom offchain data, instant or short-notice upgrades and a nonfunctional proof system. FRAX emissions can outpace fee demand. Flox activity may disappear when rewards decline. Official pages also mix current L2 facts, future L1 plans, stale FXTL promises and multiple renamed Frax assets. We lack a clean supply reconciliation, repeat-user cohorts, incentive-adjusted fees and beneficial-control map.

lifecycle.body: Fraxtal is operating but declining. The chain, bridge, FRAX gas and Flox rewards are live, and monthly trading rebounded. TVL is still 79.18% below peak, stablecoins are below TVL, activity is low and retained revenue was under $1,000 for the reviewed month. This is a functioning ecosystem chain that has not yet converted its integrated Frax distribution into durable broad demand.

outlook_and_watch.body: The base case is a small Frax-centered L2 that remains useful to its home ecosystem but struggles to attract demand beyond incentives. The call improves if proofs become functional, data and upgrade controls strengthen, TVL and repeat users stabilize, and fees grow faster than FRAX emissions. Watch sequencer and proposer changes, DA retrieval, proof deployment, FXTL treatment, FRAX supply and burns, Flox concentration, TVL, users and retained revenue.

what_it_is.body: GalaChain is a non-EVM Layer 1 built on Hyperledger Fabric for games and entertainment. Applications use TypeScript chaincode and REST APIs rather than standard EVM RPC. GalaChain is the base network; Gala Games, Music, Film, GalaSwap and individual titles are products that use it. Current docs describe managed infrastructure and authoritative nodes. Future Founder Node workloads are not the current consensus model.

what_happened.body: GalaChain supports live products and recorded $87.87 million of thirty-day DEX volume, but that volume had fallen 93.38% from the prior provider comparison. TVL was $3.60 million, 85.12% below its January 2026 peak of $24.21 million. Fees were $267,059 and provider-reported retained revenue was zero. GALA traded at $0.00179913 with an $88.49 million market capitalization, 99.78% below its recorded high.

why_this_outcome.body: Gala built a chain around an existing entertainment distribution funnel and optimized for managed performance instead of open EVM compatibility. That made onboarding Gala-owned products easier and produced meaningful trading. It also limited standard node and tooling participation and tied demand closely to one company’s product slate. Current capital, volume and token drawdowns show that product integrations have not created durable broad market demand. The chain is live but declining.

strategic_choices.body: Gala chose Hyperledger Fabric and managed authoritative nodes instead of an open EVM validator network. It chose REST gateways and organization identities for application integration, while users still sign with secp256k1 keys. It built a common token and chaincode framework for its own product portfolio, and opened chaincode deployment first on public testnet. Broader mainnet participation and Founder Node workloads remain separate future steps.

operating_model.body: Authoritative Hyperledger Fabric nodes execute chaincode. End users sign requests, then GalaChain REST services call chaincode with Fabric CA identities; organization MSP rules and user-key checks both authorize execution. Exchanges cannot run local nodes and instead use public APIs. This can deliver predictable application performance, but it makes gateway, organization, ordering and upgrade control central to the security model.

token_and_value_capture.body: GALA is used across the Gala ecosystem and is the market asset associated with GalaChain, but chain fees, game sales, NFT trades and company revenue are different flows. CoinGecko observed 49.18 billion GALA circulating against a 50 billion maximum, with an $88.49 million market capitalization and similar fully diluted value. Provider-reported chain fees do not establish how much value reaches node operators, developers, token holders or the company.

counterfactual.body: Gala could have launched an EVM chain with open node software, gaining standard wallets, contracts and exchange infrastructure while giving up some managed control. It could have deployed its products on an existing chain, avoiding base-layer cost but losing a custom entertainment platform. It could also make Founder Nodes part of ordering sooner, broadening participation while increasing coordination and performance risk.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The main risks are authoritative-node and gateway concentration, organization credential compromise, mainnet deployment control, first-party product dependence and unclear fee allocation. GalaSwap volume may be concentrated and is not a user count. Zero provider revenue does not mean the broader Gala business earned nothing. We lack unique-user retention, independent node ownership, ordering rules, upgrade powers, product-level economics and a chain-to-company revenue reconciliation.

lifecycle.body: GalaChain is operating but declining. It runs live entertainment products and still records trading and fees. TVL is 85.12% below peak, monthly DEX volume fell 93.38%, provider revenue was zero and GALA is 99.78% below its high. The next test is whether outside developers and repeat users create demand that is not dependent on first-party launches or short trading cycles.

outlook_and_watch.body: The base case is a managed entertainment chain that remains useful to Gala’s own products but has difficulty proving a broad independent developer economy. The call improves if outside applications ship, repeat wallets grow, volume diversifies and fee allocation becomes transparent. Watch mainnet deployment access, node and orderer ownership, Founder Node workloads, active users by product, GalaSwap concentration, GALA supply, fees and retained chain revenue.

outcome.label: declining
outcome.summary: GalaChain is a live managed entertainment L1 with meaningful trading, but capital, monthly volume and GALA are deeply below peak and retained chain revenue is unproven. It is operating and declining.

why.summary: First-party distribution and managed infrastructure shipped products quickly, while closed node integration and dependence on one entertainment ecosystem did not create durable broad demand.

strategic_choices.decision: Build on managed Hyperledger Fabric rather than an open EVM validator network.
strategic_choices.consequence: Gala gains configurable application performance while limiting standard tooling and independent operation.

strategic_choices.decision: Expose REST gateways and organization authorization.
strategic_choices.consequence: Applications integrate through familiar APIs while depending on Gala-operated access and Fabric identities.

strategic_choices.decision: Use first-party entertainment products as initial distribution.
strategic_choices.consequence: The chain ships with users and content but remains tied to Gala’s own portfolio.

counterfactual.summary: An open EVM network would improve composability; deploying on an existing chain would reduce base-layer cost; earlier Founder Node ordering would broaden participation. Each alternative gives up managed performance, sovereignty or simplicity.

watch.signal: Repeat users by product, outside applications, TVL, volume, fees and retained revenue.
watch.implication: Diversified durable demand would show GalaChain is more than first-party infrastructure.

watch.signal: Mainnet deployment access, node and orderer ownership, Founder Node workloads and GALA supply.
watch.implication: Broader verifiable control and clearer economics would improve the network case.

what_it_is.body: Internet Computer is a blockchain compute network made of many subnet blockchains. Applications run in canisters that pay for computation and storage with cycles. ICP is used for governance, node rewards and conversion into cycles. Replicated update calls change state; faster query calls can answer without consensus and therefore have different trust properties. DeFi is one workload on ICP, not the whole network.

what_happened.body: The official dashboard API reported 1,158,254 running canisters, 86 subnets, 103 node providers, 1,558 rewardable nodes and about 4,781 message executions per second at review. At the same time, DeFi TVL was $12.39 million, 88.82% below its April 2024 peak, and thirty-day DEX volume was $6.87 million, up 74.8% from a low base. ICP traded at $2.11, 99.70% below its launch-era recorded high.

why_this_outcome.body: ICP pursued a harder product than a conventional smart-contract chain: hosting application code, state, web content and cross-chain signing across specialized subnets. That strategy produced substantial canister and message activity that DeFi TVL does not capture. It also created unfamiliar tooling, governance and token economics, while the market launched at an extreme price and later repriced sharply. The fair call is middling: meaningful technical use, weak capital and token outcomes.

strategic_choices.body: ICP chose horizontally scaled subnets and canister-based application hosting instead of one global execution chain. It chose the NNS to control protocol upgrades, node membership and economic parameters, with application-specific SNS governance available separately. It also converts ICP into cycles for compute and uses chain-key threshold cryptography to interact with other networks without a conventional wrapped-asset bridge.

operating_model.body: Each subnet is a replicated blockchain run by a selected set of node machines. The NNS adds providers, assigns nodes, upgrades protocol software and sets economic parameters through governance proposals. Update calls go through consensus and execution; query calls can be served without consensus for speed and need certified responses when authenticity matters. The network had reached its stated target topology, so new nodes were not being onboarded automatically.

token_and_value_capture.body: ICP is minted for node-provider and voting rewards and burned when converted into cycles. Canisters spend cycles for computation, memory and calls, so real application usage creates token demand indirectly through the cycles market. The dashboard observed a 39.58 billion cycles-per-second burn rate. CoinGecko observed a $1.17 billion ICP market capitalization and fully diluted value. DeFi fees are only one small part of this value-capture path.

counterfactual.body: ICP could have focused on an EVM-compatible monolithic chain, improving familiar DeFi tooling while abandoning much of the onchain-compute thesis. It could let providers join without NNS approval, broadening access while making subnet quality and topology harder to manage. It could also separate compute credits from ICP conversion, simplifying price exposure for developers while weakening direct token burn.

risks_and_unknowns.body: ICP’s risks are NNS voting concentration, provider and data-center concentration, subnet-specific failures, complex cross-subnet behavior, query-response authenticity and inflation that can exceed cycles burn. Raw canister and message counts may include inactive or machine-heavy workloads and are not unique users. We lack an independent entity-level governance map, retained-user cohorts, application revenue, cycles burn by workload and a simple reconciliation of minting versus burn.

lifecycle.body: Internet Computer is operating and middling. More than one million running canisters, thousands of message executions per second and 86 subnets show a substantial live compute system. DeFi TVL is 88.82% below peak, DEX activity is small and ICP is 99.70% below its recorded high. The network succeeded at shipping a distinct technical platform but has not translated that platform into strong DeFi capital or token performance.

outlook_and_watch.body: The base case is a durable specialist compute network whose application activity remains much larger than its DeFi footprint. The call improves if cycles burn grows faster than ICP issuance, active canisters and users retain, governance control broadens and applications earn repeat revenue. Watch running versus stopped canisters, messages, cycles burn, subnet capacity, provider diversity, NNS voting power, node rewards, ICP mint and burn, developer retention and application-level revenue.

outcome.summary: Internet Computer runs a substantial multi-subnet compute network, while its DeFi capital and token remain deeply below peak. Its technical platform is meaningfully used, but the overall outcome is mixed.

why.summary: Subnet compute, canisters and chain-key integration created a distinct product, while unfamiliar tooling, governed infrastructure and weak capital and token demand limited broader market success.

strategic_choices.decision: Scale through subnet blockchains and canister hosting.
strategic_choices.consequence: ICP supports broad compute workloads while introducing cross-subnet and operational complexity.

strategic_choices.decision: Use the NNS for protocol, node and economic governance.
strategic_choices.consequence: The network can upgrade coherently while making voting-power distribution central to trust.

strategic_choices.decision: Convert ICP into cycles and use chain-key threshold cryptography.
strategic_choices.consequence: Compute demand can burn ICP and external-chain actions avoid conventional wrapped bridges, but the model is harder to evaluate.

counterfactual.summary: An EVM-first monolithic chain would improve familiarity; open node entry would broaden access; separate compute credits would reduce developer price exposure. Each alternative gives up specialization, topology control or token burn.

watch.signal: Running and stopped canisters, messages, cycles burn, active users and application revenue.
watch.implication: Retained paid compute demand would prove product-market fit beyond raw object counts.

watch.signal: Subnet capacity, provider diversity, NNS voting power, node rewards and ICP mint versus burn.
watch.implication: Broader control and improving supply economics would strengthen the network and token case.

unknowns.question: How many running canisters serve retained human users?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A multi-quarter application and wallet cohort.

unknowns.question: Who ultimately controls effective NNS voting power?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: An entity-level delegation and following map.

unknowns.question: Does cycles burn exceed combined node and voting issuance?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A monthly audited mint, burn and reward reconciliation.

unknowns.question: How concentrated are node providers and subnet failure domains?
unknowns.resolution_trigger: A current ownership, data-center and jurisdiction map.
